source_evidence.observation: For a random variable X, properties (a)--(d) are declared equivalent. Their positive parameters may change, but any property i with parameter K_i implies any property j with some K_j at most a universal absolute constant times K_i.
Property (c), whose parameter is K3, requires E exp(lambda |X|) <= exp(K3 lambda) for every lambda in the one-sided interval 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3.
Property (d), whose parameter is K4, requires the single-point bound E exp(|X|/K4) <= 2.
The source assigns the proof of equivalence of properties (a)--(d) as an exercise, explicitly tying Definition 2.7.5 to Proposition 2.7.1.
A random variable satisfying one of Proposition 2.7.1(a)--(d) is called sub-exponential.
The prose defines the sub-exponential norm as the smallest K3 in property 3, which structurally points to the K3 parameter of the third listed property, Proposition 2.7.1(c).

source_evidence.anchor: Display (2.21) introduced by the words 'In other words'
source_evidence.observation: The displayed formula instead sets the psi_1 norm equal to inf {t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2}, which has exactly the form of property (d), with t in the role of K4.

binders: A real-valued random variable X on the ambient probability space.
Positive real parameters K1, K2, K3, and K4 for the four equivalent sub-exponential properties.
For property (a), a real threshold t >= 0; for property (b), a real moment order p >= 1; for property (c), a real lambda with 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3.
hypotheses: For the classification clause, X satisfies at least one of Proposition 2.7.1(a)--(d); by the proposition this is equivalent, up to an absolute-factor change of parameter, to satisfying each of the other three.
The norm discussion is made for a sub-exponential random variable X.
conclusions: Such an X is called a sub-exponential random variable.
The prose clause defines ||X||_{psi_1} to be the smallest admissible K3 in property (c): E exp(lambda |X|) <= exp(K3 lambda) for all 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3.
Separately, display (2.21) states ||X||_{psi_1} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2}, the infimum gauge arising from property (d).

The source presents the preceding prose clause and display (2.21) as exact restatements, even though Proposition 2.7.1 supplies only equivalence up to an absolute constant factor between properties (c) and (d).
definitions_and_conventions: Property (a): P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t/K1) for all t >= 0.
Property (b): ||X||_{L^p} = (E |X|^p)^(1/p) <= K2 p for all p >= 1.
Property (c): E exp(lambda |X|) <= exp(K3 lambda) for all lambda satisfying 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3.
Equivalence of properties means parameter conversion within one universal absolute constant factor, not equality of the four numerical parameters.
The name psi_1 norm and notation ||X||_{psi_1} are introduced in Definition 2.7.5.
implicit_context: Probability and expectation are taken in the ambient probability space of X.
The random variable is real-valued, as shown by the use of |X| and the surrounding chapter conventions.
No centering assumption E X = 0 is part of Definition 2.7.5; the centered property (e) in Proposition 2.7.1 is outside the definition's stated range (a)--(d).
The absolute conversion constant in the proposition is universal and independent of X, the parameter values, and the pair of properties.

details: Membership in the sub-exponential class is independent of which one of properties (a)--(d) is used, subject to absolute-factor parameter conversion.
Definition 2.7.5 does not require the centered MGF property (e).
The admissibility condition is uniform over the full one-sided lambda interval [0, 1/K3].
The right-hand side varies with lambda as exp(K3 lambda).
Negative lambda values are not included.
The displayed admissibility test is at the single point 1/t.
The displayed quantity is an infimum over strictly positive t.
The prose identifies the norm with the property-(c) parameter K3.
The displayed formula identifies it with the property-(d) infimum gauge.
The proposition justifies comparison up to an absolute factor but does not justify literal equality of these two gauge definitions.

undebatable_constraints: Sub-exponential classification must use the four properties (a)--(d), not require centered property (e).
The property named by the prose as K3/property 3 is property (c), with a universal quantifier over 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3 and right-hand side exp(K3 lambda).
Property (c) is one-sided in lambda; extending it to negative lambda is explicitly warned against in Exercise 2.7.4.
Display (2.21) must retain the strict domain t > 0, the expectation E exp(|X|/t), the bound 2, and the infimum.
The property-(c) gauge and display-(2.21) gauge must be kept distinct when reporting the literal source; their source-provided relationship is equivalence only up to an absolute constant factor.
No assumption of independence, identical distribution, or zero mean belongs to this definition.

ambiguities.issue: The list is lettered (a)--(d), while the norm prose says 'property 3'; the accompanying symbol K3 makes the intended literal reference property (c), but the numbering terminology itself is inconsistent.
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.7.5 says smallest K3 in property 3; Proposition 2.7.1 assigns K3 to its third item, labeled (c).
ambiguities.impact: A formal target following the prose should use the property-(c) admissibility condition, not infer the displayed property-(d) gauge merely from the phrase 'property 3'.

ambiguities.issue: The sentence introducing (2.21) claims an exact restatement, but the prose and display use different equivalent properties and different numerical thresholds.
ambiguities.evidence: Property (c) imposes E exp(lambda |X|) <= exp(K3 lambda) for every lambda in [0,1/K3], whereas (2.21) imposes E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 at one point. Proposition 2.7.1 states only absolute-factor equivalence of their parameters.
ambiguities.impact: The source does not support treating the property-(c) infimum and the displayed property-(d) infimum as exactly equal. An audit must preserve this discrepancy or explicitly select one clause under a correction policy.

ambiguities.issue: The prose uses 'smallest' K3, while the displayed clause is written as an infimum and the source does not separately prove attainment for the prose-defined property-(c) parameter.
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.7.5 uses the word smallest immediately before an infimum formula for a different admissibility predicate.
ambiguities.impact: A literal formal reconstruction of the prose may safely identify an infimum/least-bound gauge only with an explicit convention or proof of attainment; the source passage itself leaves this point unstated.

contract_plain_english: Definition 2.7.5 calls X sub-exponential when it has any of the equivalent tail, moment, local absolute-MGF, or one-point exponential-moment properties (a)--(d). Its prose then says that ||X||_{psi_1} is the smallest K3 satisfying the local property-(c) estimate uniformly for 0 <= lambda <= 1/K3. The immediately following display (2.21), however, defines an infimum of t for the one-point property-(d) bound E exp(|X|/t) <= 2. These gauges are comparable up to a universal constant by Proposition 2.7.1, but the source does not establish that they are literally equal; the contract therefore records both clauses and the discrepancy.
